item.title: Discarded Needles/Sharps on grassed island on John Harrison Way near the junction with West Parkside/Hendon Street, 9th September
item.description:
Approximately 3–5 discarded needles/syringes are present on the public grassed/pedestrian area on John Harrison Way, immediately outside/adjacent to a secondary school, near the junction with West Parkside/Hendon Street. I have noticed an increasing number appearing in this location over the past 1–2 weeks. This area is accessible to school pupils and members of the public, being not only on the island in the middle of the road but down the side of the curb too. These are potentially contaminated sharps and I have not touched or moved them. Please arrange safe removal and check the surrounding area for additional needles.

item.title: Dudrich Mews-Flytipping-3rd complaint-Legal Issues, 9th September
item.description:
2 matresses not being removed at Dudrich Mews entrance While it is acknowledged that Section 59(1) of the Environmental Protection Act 1990 (EPA 1990) places a duty on landowners to clear waste, you have the legal authority—and a statutory duty—to enforce this. Your claim that you are "unable to take any action" is factually incorrect. You are choosing not to act. To rectify this, it is requested that you immediately take the following two actions: 1. **Use your enforcement powers under Section 59(2) of the EPA 1990** The law explicitly allows the council to serve a notice on the landowner/occupier requiring the removal of the waste. If they fail to comply, you may enter the land, clear it, and recover your costs from them . 2. **Use Section 215 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990** If the waste is adversely affecting the amenity of the area (which it invariably does), you can serve a "Section 215 Notice" requiring the land to be cleaned up . Failure to comply is a criminal offence punishable by an unlimited fine . Regarding the "Private Land" excuse: The Clean Neighbourhoods and Environment Act 2005 and subsequent case law confirm that councils cannot simply "close the case" because land is privately owned. Your duty to investigate the perpetrator (the tipper) remains active regardless of land ownership. **Conclusion:** If the waste constitutes a "statutory nuisance" (e.g., attracts rats, smells, or poses a health risk), you have a positive duty to act under the Environmental Protection Act 1990 . Failure to do so could result in a potential breach of duty, which will be referred to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman for "maladministration" where failure to investigate amid potential criminal offences in some reports by the public was only conducted in 1 minute .

Nearest road to the pin placed on the map (automatically generated by OpenStreetMap): Dudrich Mews, East Dulwich, Greater London
Report on FixMyStreet
